source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.
prompt:
You are assisting with a scholarly experiment in structural literary analysis.

TASK: Write an ORIGINAL short prose passage in English, set in the target scenario below. It must be
a HOMEOSYNTACTIC transposition of a hidden source: hold the source's syntactic form at the level
specified below while inventing entirely new words and moving the content into the target
scenario. It is NOT a paraphrase or a translation.

FORM TARGET (hold this). Reproduce, period by period, the CLAUSE-NESTING SCHEMA below --- an indented tree in which each line is a clause (main / relative / adverbial / complement / coordinate) and indentation marks subordination (a clause indented under another is embedded in it). Hold the SAME nesting: the same clauses, each embedded under the same kind of parent clause, to the same depth. The WORD ORDER and the words themselves are entirely yours; only the clause-embedding tree is fixed.
Reproduce it for all 10 periods, in this order:
Period 1 (about 8 words) clause-nesting schema:
  - main clause
Period 2 (about 29 words) clause-nesting schema:
  - main clause
    - open complement (infinitive)
    - adverbial clause
Period 3 (about 3 words) clause-nesting schema:
  - main clause
Period 4 (about 15 words) clause-nesting schema:
  - main clause
    - relative/adnominal clause
Period 5 (about 11 words) clause-nesting schema:
  - main clause
    - adverbial clause
      - relative/adnominal clause
Period 6 (about 9 words) clause-nesting schema:
  - main clause
    - relative/adnominal clause
      - open complement (infinitive)
Period 7 (about 12 words) clause-nesting schema:
  - main clause
    - adverbial clause
Period 8 (about 18 words) clause-nesting schema:
  - main clause
Period 9 (about 19 words) clause-nesting schema:
  - main clause
    - relative/adnominal clause
      - finite complement clause
        - open complement (infinitive)
          - relative/adnominal clause
Period 10 (about 9 words) clause-nesting schema:
  - main clause
    - finite complement clause

TARGET SCENARIO --- render the content here (in your own words):
  - an airport/border security checkpoint at a busy hour
  - the queue and the barriers; the divestment of belongings into trays
  - the scanners, metal detectors, and the body-search gesture
  - an officer and a traveller singled out of the line; documents and a wanded pat-down
  - the register of control: instructions, signage, the impersonal courtesy of authority

REQUIREMENTS --- both hold together:
1. CLAUSE NESTING PRESERVED --- the same clause-embedding tree per period (which clause embeds in which, to the same depth), in any word order and words you choose.
2. COHERENT --- one continuous, fully sensible passage in the target scenario; new lexicon,
   no trace of any source content.

Write modern, natural English. Produce the 10 periods in order as continuous prose --- no
numbering, no headings. Output ONLY the passage: no preamble, no self-audit.

gens.text:
The morning line coiled toward the barriers.

Travelers shuffled forward to empty their pockets into gray trays, while the belts hummed and swallowed each bag in turn.

The scanner glowed.

An officer watched the monitor that flickered with the pale shadows of a hundred packed suitcases.

She paused when a shape appeared that no one could quite name.

A man was chosen to step aside.

His documents were checked while the crowd pressed on behind him.

The wand traced the length of his arms and hovered near his belt with a small mechanical whine.

He stood beneath a sign that instructed everyone that they were required to remove the shoes that airport policy had long deemed suspect.

The officer murmured that the delay was routine.

The line grew long before the barriers.

Travelers began to unload their pockets, to surrender their coats and laptops into the gray plastic trays, while the officer near the belt gestured them forward one by one.

The queue crept.

A woman ahead of me lifted a bag that would not fit the opening.

The scanner hummed a warning whenever a shape it disliked crossed the screen.

Someone waved a passenger aside, a passenger asked to stand apart.

An officer approached me once the detector chimed at my belt.

The wand traced the length of each arm and swept slowly down along both legs in the impersonal choreography of the search.

A sign above the lane repeated the notice that all passengers must accept to be examined by staff whose questions no one dared refuse.

The officer said quietly that everything was in order.

The line inches forward under the bright signs. Travelers begin to loosen their coats, to empty their pockets into the gray trays, while the loudspeaker repeats its calm instructions above the shuffle. Belts come off. A woman removes the laptop that her hands had been guarding all morning. She hesitates at the belt because the tray in front of her keeps stalling. An officer steps near, gesturing her to lift her arms. The metal detector chimes when a stranger passes through it. The wand hovers along a shoulder, along a hip, along the seam of a folded sleeve. A second traveler is pulled aside by a guard whose eyes suggest that he intends to check the badge that everyone else ignored. They insist that the search means nothing.

The line coiled toward the barriers. Travelers stooped to unload their pockets, shedding belts and watches into gray trays, while the loudspeaker recited its instructions overhead. Signs glowed everywhere. A guard beckoned the next passenger, whose bag had already vanished into the scanner. The detector chimed sharply when a man whose keys remained hidden stepped through. An officer approached, ready to wand him thoroughly. Everyone shuffled forward once the tray cleared the belt. The impersonal courtesy of the checkpoint softened nothing, and the queue pressed on regardless. She was the one whom the officer decided that he should search, patting shoulders that his gloved hands mapped methodically. The screen confirmed that nothing remained.

The line curled back against the barrier ropes. Travelers shuffled forward, waiting to shed their belongings into the gray trays, while an amplified voice repeated the same rules overhead. Coats, then laptops. A conveyor swallowed each tray that slid beneath the scanner's dark mouth. The detector chimed whenever a passenger who had forgotten some coin walked through. An officer stepped near, motioning for me to halt. She wanded my shoulders slowly, because the alarm had sounded twice. Her gloved hands traced my sleeves and belt with a brisk, indifferent politeness. She examined the boarding pass I carried, murmuring that I ought to wait beside the counter that faced the glass. The signage above insisted that all cooperation was appreciated.

The line coiled toward the barriers.

Travelers shuffled forward to surrender their pockets while the overhead speakers repeated the same clipped announcement.

Trays slid outward.

A man ahead of me stacked the belongings that he had carried loose.

Belts loosened everywhere as the officer whose gloves gleamed waved us on.

She gestured at a passenger reluctant to raise his arms.

The wand rose and fell whenever the detector chirped.

The impersonal courtesy of the badge softened nothing about the search itself.

The traveler singled from the queue understood that the papers he offered would fail to satisfy an inspector who nodded at nothing.

The signage insisted that compliance was expected.

The morning line coiled past the barriers. Travelers shuffled forward, hoping to reach the belt before the announcement repeated, while an officer waved the next group through. Trays slid out. A woman emptied her pockets into the bin that waited at the mouth of the scanner. She hesitated when the light above the arch, which had blinked amber, held steady. A guard stepped near, ready to gesture. Bags rolled onward as the machine hummed its dull refrain. Signs above the counter thanked us all with a flat, unbending, unarguable politeness. A man was drawn from the crowd by a supervisor who murmured that he ought to remove the belt whose buckle had triggered the alarm. Everyone understood that the wand would decide.

The line coils past the barriers. Travelers begin to empty their pockets, to lay their belongings into gray trays, before the belt draws each case beneath the scanner's cold arch. Signs command silence. A woman ahead of me clutches a passport that has softened at its corners. She hesitates when the light above the detector, which nobody trusts, flashes red. An officer steps forward, gesturing for her to raise her arms. He waves the wand along her sleeves as the machine beeps twice. Documents change hands with the impersonal courtesy of a rehearsed phrase, neither warm nor unkind. She stands there, exposed, sensing that the whole apparatus expects her to become someone who has nothing left to conceal. The overhead voice reminds us that all bags remain the owner's responsibility.

The line coiled toward the barriers.

Travelers began to shed their belongings into the gray trays, unlacing their shoes and surrendering their laptops, because the signs above demanded a total emptying of pockets.

The scanners hummed.

An officer in a blue uniform watched the archway that swallowed each passenger in turn.

A man beeped twice as he passed through the frame that catalogued every buckle.

She stepped forward to wave a wand across his shoulders.

His documents lay open on the counter while she traced the contour of his belt.

The pat-down was brisk, courteous, entirely impersonal, a choreography rehearsed ten thousand times a day.

He nodded at the instruction, a clipped courtesy that told him he was free to gather the possessions that the machine had scattered.

The signage insisted that all cooperation was appreciated.

The queue folded back on itself twice.

Travelers shuffled forward to surrender their coats and phones, while the overhead speakers repeated the same clipped announcement about liquids and laptops.

The line barely moved.

A bored officer waved the next passenger toward the tray-stacked table that fed the scanner belt.

Everything slowed whenever a bag stalled inside the machine that some trainee kept reloading.

A red light flagged the man who had forgotten to empty his pockets.

Belts and shoes went off as the arch beeped twice.

An agent lifted her wand and gestured him aside with the flat, practiced courtesy of a rehearsed apology.

She held out a hand for the passport that the notice above her insisted every visitor must present in order to enter the corridor that led onward.

The signs promised that cooperation would speed things along.
